k-1.x_notes: Ten problems that are all correct and all hands-on with counters: choose 1st/2nd for piles 3-6 under {1,2} (answers 2nd at 3 and 6); find the winning move at 4, 5, 7, 8; classify piles 1-12 under {1,2}, {1,2,3} and {1,3} (losing piles are multiples of 3, multiples of 4, and evens); beat greedy Ben (you win at 3, 4, 6, 7 but not at 2 or 5); pile of 20 under three rules; two-pile pairs (2,2), (1,2), (3,3), (1,4), where (1,4) being a second-player win is a nice surprise. The material is not dumbed down and lasts the full time. P9 and P10 each get their own large ringing board with enough rows (5 games of 4, 8 games of 5), and P9 has one ringed 2+2 row as a recording example, which a non-reader needs. P10 adds 'star each game the first player wins', which links counting the games back to who wins (an odd number of turns). Weaknesses: 'Your partner plays Ben' is slightly ambiguous, and 'Shade' is slower than circling for 12 boxes. Footer has no id.
k-1.y_notes: Problems 1-8 are almost the same as X's and all correct. P1 starts at a pile of 2, which is a gentler first entry. It uses 'Circle' throughout, which is quicker for young children, and P4's wording ('Circle each pile where you can beat Ben when he goes first') is a bit clearer. P9 and P10 share one page in side-by-side narrow boards with enough rows. There is no example of how to record a game by ringing, which kindergartners will need an adult to show. P10 is only enumeration, without X's link back to who wins. Footer has no id.
k-1.reason: The two are nearly identical and both correct. X's sample ringed row and its 'star the games the first player wins' task make the final enumeration problems easier for K-1 to start and add more mathematics, which slightly outweighs Y's gentler P1 and simpler circling.

grades-2-3.x_notes: This band has the same strong, correct sequence in both packets. P1 classifies piles under {1,2}. P2 tests four plans under {1,2}: Mia and Ana always win, while Leo and Sam can lose. P3 builds the 1-20 table for {1,3,4}, where the losing piles are 2, 7, 9, 14, 16. P4 extrapolates to 25, 30, 37, 50 (answers 1st, 2nd, 2nd, 1st). P5 tests plans under {1,3,4}: greedy Kai and copycat Theo can lose, and Zoe's 'leave 7 or 2' plan wins every time. P6 is Jon's claim, which is false because {1,2,4} also gives multiples of 3. P7 is two-pile pairs (5,5), (3,6), (2,5) as second-player wins and (1,5) as a first-player win. In X, 'The pile has 8 counters' reads clearly. P6 explicitly asks 'how you can be sure, even for piles bigger than 15', which pushes toward the general argument. P6 and P7 each get a full page with a large box for the explanation.
grades-2-3.y_notes: The problems and answers are the same and all correct. P6 has a well-aligned two-row comparison table, which makes the comparison easy. The wording 'I start with 8 counters' is slightly less clear, since it can sound as if Mia owns 8 counters. P6 asks only 'Explain how you know', so the generalization beyond 15 is left to the adult. P6 and P7 share a page with small explanation boxes.
grades-2-3.reason: The mathematics is identical. X's explicit push to explain why the pattern holds beyond 15, together with roomier space for the explanations, gives it a slight edge over Y's neater but tighter P6/P7 page.

grades-4-5.x_notes: The problems are rich and correct. P1 and P2 cover {1,2} and {1,3,4}, the latter with an explanation of why its period-7 pattern continues. P3 has seven rules with the coinciding pairs {1,2}/{1,2,4}, {1,3}/{1,3,5} and {1,4}/{1,4,6}. In P4, greedy Kai is never wrong only for {1,3} and {1,3,5}. P5 is inverse design: {1,2,3,4}, {1,4,5} and {1,2,6} work, and 3,5,8,10,... is impossible. P6 is {1,6,9}, where 9 breaks the pattern and the period 5 starts at 10, plus a pigeonhole proof. Then come two-pile grids and the mex labels. The ordering finishes the repeating-pattern kernel (P6) before moving to sums. That matters because three children will not finish nine problems, and grades 4-5 are meant to focus on patterns. P8 asks for losing pairs of different sizes, and P9 asks how the labels 'tell you which pairs in your grid from Problem 8 are losing', which gives a purpose to the abstract labels. Answers: 11 and 13 is a losing pair, 12 and 18 a winning pair. Circling numbers in P3 is laid out spaciously.
grades-4-5.y_notes: The problems and answers are the same and all correct. P4's wording ('leaves his partner a winning pile') is more precise, P5 adds a useful one-line definition of 'rule', and P3's single-row 24-cell strips line up well for comparison. However, the {1,6,9} eventual-periodicity problem and the general argument for why patterns repeat are placed last (P9), after the two-pile and label problems, so the central 4-5 idea is the one most likely to go unreached. P8 introduces the labels with no prompt connecting them to the P7 grid, so children may not see why they are computing them unless an adult steps in. P7 asks only 'which pairs are losing'.
grades-4-5.reason: The content is the same, but X's order puts the eventual-periodicity problem where this group will reach it, and its P8-P9 wording ties the labels to the two-pile grid, so the Sprague-Grundy idea has a purpose. Y's small wording improvements count for less.

overall.reason: The two packets are close variants with the same correct mathematics and clean, organizer-compliant pages. In every band X makes small choices that help in the room: a recording example and a winner link for K-1, a push to generalize and room to explain for 2-3, and better sequencing and a purposeful bridge to Sprague-Grundy labels for 4-5. Either would work after a short edit, but X needs less.
